r3-p10-000: Stage-1 design — foam-board model and mass conditions
r3-p10-001: 100 g weights at L/4 and 3L/4 create three conditions: 0-0 (normal), 1-0 (left) and 1-1 (both sides).
r3-p10-002: Stage-2 design — aluminum multi-span model and a 27-condition matrix
r3-p10-003: The factors below are run as a matrix of 3 environment states × 3 mass levels × 3 bolt levels = 27 conditions. Because the heater changes temperature and humidity at the same time, temperature alone cannot be changed; the environment therefore has three states: no change (Tx-Hx), humidity change (Tx-Ho) and temperature/humidity change (To-Ho). This design yields interaction data between environment (T·H) and simulated damage (M·B), and tests the value of temperature/humidity compensation, which should classify environmental change as normal and damage as anomalous.
r3-p10-010: Tx-Hx = no environmental input. Tx-Ho = high humidity in an opaque box with a humidifier (temperature
r3-p10-011: held). To-Ho = heater raises temperature and lowers humidity. Analysis uses DHT22
r3-p10-015: At two marks, x = 150 and 450 mm: M500 = 500 g on one side (asymmetric); M1000 = 500 g
r3-p10-016: on each side (symmetric). 50 g weights stacked in the same order every time
r3-p10-020: Deck–beam through-bolts loosened by 1/2 turn from fully tightened. B1 = one left
r3-p10-021: bolt (asymmetric); B2 = left and right (symmetric boundary damage)
r3-p10-022: Loosening is limited to the deck–beam through-bolts, which act directly on the deck's boundary conditions, and B1 is a subset of B2 so that boundary stiffness is lowered step by step. After the bolt conditions, the original tightening is restored to check that the anomaly score returns to baseline. The normal class is defined as the three M0·B0 cells (three environment states), so that a state in which only the environment changed is learned as normal; because these cells are used for training and thresholding, they are collected longer than the other conditions.
r3-p10-023: The runs are grouped into three environment blocks, each containing the 9 mass × bolt conditions. Each condition receives 10 warm-up taps (not recorded) followed by 35 recorded taps; each of the three normal cells receives 180 recorded taps. The normal cells are split in time order into 120 training, 30 threshold and 30 evaluation windows, giving 360 training, 90 threshold and 90 evaluation windows in total.
r3-p10-024: Stage-3 design — field measurement on real bridges
r3-p10-025: Ambient vibration was measured for 30 minutes on each of five candidate overpasses (A–E) and compared as in the table below. E (1.74 Hz) and C (3.81 Hz), whose dominant peaks stand out more than 10,000-fold over the band median, were selected; D, with no visible peak, A, with too little vibration, and B, with impulsive vibration mixed in, were excluded. E, where several days of observation were possible, was assigned to environmental validation, and C, where loading was possible, to detection-power validation.
r3-p10-042: Excitation is the ambient vibration from pedestrians and vehicles, and a deck surface-temperature sensor (DS18B20) was added to the single node. Bridge E, assigned to environmental validation, was recorded in 7 sessions over 4 days, September 7–10, for about 68 hours. Because damage cannot be inflicted on a real bridge, recall is not computed; the normal state is assumed on the basis of the most recent inspection grade, and threshold exceedances are treated as false alarms. The main indicators are the mode
r3-p11-000: html:peak reproducibility, the false-alarm rate when one session's threshold is applied unchanged to the other sessions, and the temperature sensitivity of the peak frequency. Bridge C, assigned to detection power, was used for a reversible added-mass test; preliminary measurements in three sessions with the same mounting on September 20 (about 6 hours) identified the peak to track. The required weight follows from the frequency being proportional to √(stiffness/mass). If M<sub>eq</sub> is the equivalent mass that acts effectively on the mode at the loading position, a weight m much smaller than this lowers the frequency by a fraction of about m/2M<sub>eq</sub>, so the weight needed for a target reduction δ well above the measurement error is m ≈ 2δM<sub>eq</sub>. Since M<sub>eq</sub> cannot be known without drawings, a small weight m<sub>p</sub> permitted on site is loaded first, M<sub>eq</sub> ≈ m<sub>p</sub> / ((f<sub>0</sub>/f<sub>p</sub>)<sup>2</sup> − 1) is back-calculated from the unloaded and loaded frequencies f<sub>0</sub> and f<sub>p</sub>, and the main-test mass is then chosen.
r3-p11-015: The stage-3 acquisition program and logging intervals are as in 2.2, without condition codes. Each session's raw CSV has columns for timestamp, DHT22 air temperature and relative humidity, DS18B20 surface temperature, ADXL355Z internal temperature and 3-axis acceleration in g, and is identified by the session start time in the folder name; mounting, remounting and traffic events are kept in field notes and linked to windows during analysis.
r3-p11-017: Testing is divided into analysis of the public openLAB data (2.7), our own model-bridge experiments and field measurements on real bridges. Because openLAB is undamaged throughout, it is used to compare false-alarm rates across compensation methods; our own experiments verify low-cost sensor acquisition, detection of mass change and reproduction of compensation. Only the differences between experiments are described below.
r3-p11-018: In stage 1, 0-0, 1-0 and 1-1 were excited manually and recorded repeatedly for at least 20–30 seconds per condition (3 environmental conditions, 4-second windows). The models are trained only on normal 0-0 data, and the threshold — the 99th percentile of the normal reconstruction error — is applied identically to the three models (uncompensated, temperature, temperature/humidity). All three use the PCA reconstruction of 2.3 (equivalent to a linear AE).
r3-p11-019: The key change in stage 2 is replacing manual excitation with automatic taps from the solenoid auto-tapper, which narrows the scatter of the normal baseline. Tap times and acceleration are synchronized on the same clock, and only the window right after each tap is analyzed.
r3-p11-020: Data are collected at 500 Hz sampling with a ±8 g range, and the analysis window is fixed at 2.0 s (1,000 samples) starting at t₀+0.05 s to exclude the impact. The spectrum is estimated with Welch's method, and the analysis bands were reset to 0–40, 40–80 and 80–125 Hz to match the measured dominant mode (101 Hz). The features are eight z-axis quantities (log RMS, log p2p, peak frequency, log peak power, log total energy and three band-energy ratios); amplitudes are log-scaled and band energies normalized as ratios so that changes in spectral structure, not tap strength, stand out.
r3-p11-021: Training, thresholding and evaluation are kept separate to prevent data leakage. Training uses 360 normal windows; the threshold is the 99th percentile of the reconstruction error on 90 dedicated windows not used in training; evaluation uses 90 normal and 840 damage windows. The model is fixed as a nonlinear Autoencoder with an 8–3–8 hidden structure (tanh), only the environmental inputs are varied (uncompensated, temperature, temperature/humidity), and runs are repeated with 5 random seeds to check stability.
r3-p11-022: html:In stage 3, the z-axis signal collected at 500 Hz and ±2 g is low-pass filtered at 20 Hz and downsampled to 50 Hz, and the same eight features as in stage 2 are computed with only the analysis bands reset below 20 Hz to match each bridge's dominant peak; on both bridges a 120-second window is moved in 10-second steps. The 4-second window used in the model experiments was sized for short tap records and is too short for state changes on a real bridge that last tens of minutes. For bridge E, the model is trained and its threshold set in one session and then applied unchanged to other sessions with the same mounting (also checked across remounted sessions), comparing four models: uncompensated, air temperature, air temperature + humidity, and with surface temperature added. Decisions are based on exceedances in consecutive windows, not a single window, to prevent false alarms from single events such as several people crossing at once. The alarm model for bridge C, matched to the loading test and its excitation conditions, is trained on the first 20 minutes of 30 minutes of unloaded walking at the same location on September 25 and its false-alarm rate checked on the last 10 minutes. The detection test back-calculated M<sub>eq</sub> from a 100 kg preliminary load, set the main-test mass at 200 kg, and proceeded as unloaded walking → loaded walking for 30 min → loaded heel drops (excitation by dropping the heels) → heel drops after removal (with little traffic at night, the experimenter
r3-p12-000: provided the excitation by walking). Alarms are decided by applying the model trained on unloaded walking unchanged, and the cause is judged from the drop and recovery of the frequency of the vibration that dies away on its own after a heel drop (free decay).
r3-p12-002: In stage 1, added mass is expected to lower the peak frequency, and in the asymmetric condition (1-0) changes in amplitude and band energy are expected to appear first. In stage 2, because the weights sit near the supports and their effective mass is small, the dominant-mode frequency should fall clearly but by less than the mass ratio, and bolt loosening should bring a small drop in natural frequency along with harmonics and wider peaks. The main question is whether the anomaly score rises monotonically as conditions within the same damage type become more severe (M0 → M500 → M1000, B0 → B1 → B2); this ordering must hold for the anomaly score to be usable as a severity indicator. In stage 3, as in prior work [2], the false-alarm rate of the uncompensated model is expected to grow in sessions at different temperatures and the compensated model to reduce it, although early-autumn observations do not include the cold range below 15 °C, so the effect may be small. In the added-mass test, the natural frequency is expected to drop with mass and recover after removal, with changes of about 0.4% or more distinguishable.
r3-p12-004: For the stage-1 foam-board model, the analysis bands were set to 0–12, 12–25 and 25–50 Hz to match the fundamental-mode peak in the preliminary measurement (about 22.6 Hz). Under loading on both sides (1-1) the peak frequency fell by 8.9%; under loading on one side (1-0) the peak change stayed within the scatter, but the multi-feature anomaly score detected it and the threshold-exceedance rate rose to 29.7%. In the humidity-change segment, temperature/humidity compensation reduced the false-alarm rate from 17.5% to 9.1%, and over the whole evaluation segment the compensated models were also lower than the uncompensated one (9.2% → temperature 4.8%, temperature/humidity 6.3%). The recall of the temperature/humidity-compensated model, however, was only 0.234, missing most damage windows.
r3-p12-006: The temperature/humidity-compensated model detected all 840 damage windows (recall 100%) and raised false alarms on only 4 of 90 normal evaluation windows (4.4%; ROC-AUC 0.996), all four in the simultaneous temperature/humidity (To·Ho) block (4/30 in the table below). The dominant mode of the normal baseline is 101.0 Hz, and each damage group in the table sums the three environment blocks (105 windows each). The peak shifts are far larger than expected in 3.3 (e.g., −64.4%) and even reverse (M1000·B1 −19.8%) not because the natural frequency actually fell, but because the peak frequency, which reads only the single tallest peak, jumped from the 101 Hz mode to another mode as damage changed the relative strength of the modes (mode switching, 3.5). The −10.9% in the normal heated block (To·Ho) is likewise attributed to mode switching caused by heating, not to an actual loss of stiffness.
